'''''Stenocereus griseus''''', also known as the '''Mexican organ pipe''', '''dagger cactus''', '''pitaya''', and '''pitayo de mayo''', is a species of cactus.<ref>[http://www.ipmimages.org/browse/detail.cfm?imgnum=5176067 candle cactus, Stenocereus griseus (Caryophyllales: Cactaceae)<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

==Description==

''Stenocereus griseus'' is a tree-shaped cactus that grows to 6-9 meters tall with a clear trunk and upright green stems, about 9-12 centimeters in diameter, with six to ten ribs below the areoles.<ref name=autogenerated1 /> It bears one to three central spines up to 1.5 centimeters long, the longest of which reaches 4 centimeters, and six to eleven marginal spines measuring 6-10 millimeters long.

This species produces white, funnel-shaped flowers that bloom at night and last until midday, with bent-back flower bracts. The flowers are about 10 centimeters long. Its spherical to elongated fruits are white, yellowish green, to red or dark purple, up to 5 centimeters in diameter, and covered with thorns that shed when ripe. The flesh is red.<ref name="Anderson Eggli 2005 p. 602">{{cite book | last1=Anderson | first1=Edward F. | last2=Eggli | first2=Urs | title=Das grosse Kakteen-Lexikon | publisher=Ulmer | publication-place=Stuttgart (Hohenheim) | date=2005 | isbn=3-8001-4573-1 | language=de | page=602}}</ref>

==Distribution==
This species is found in [[Mexico]] in [[Oaxaca]] and [[Veracruz]],<ref name=autogenerated1 /> coastal [[Venezuela]], Guajira Peninsula of [[Colombia]] and the [[ABC islands (Lesser Antilles)|ABC islands]] of the Dutch Caribbean.<ref>[http://cactiguide.com/cactus/?genus=Stenocereus&species=griseus Stenocereus griseus On-line Guide to the positive identification of Members of the Cactus Family<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> It is found in scrub-lands.<ref name=":0" /> Observations of this species have also been reported in the dry scrub-lands at the base of the [[Eastern Cordillera]] of the [[Colombian Andes]]. However it has not been collected in this region.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://serv.biokic.asu.edu/neotrop/plantae/taxa/index.php?taxauthid=1&taxon=93921&clid=|title=Neotropical Plant Portal - Stenocereus griseus|website=serv.biokic.asu.edu|access-date=2019-07-25}}</ref> In the Caribbean islands of Aruba, Curaçao and Bonaire, this cactus blooms and fruits profusely during the dry season. It is a critical resource for bats, birds and other animals.<ref name=":0" />

==Human uses==  
Its fruit is edible to humans and is considered good tasting. It is planted as an ornamental and as a living fence in warm regions.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Stenocereus+griseus|title=Stenocereus griseus - Useful Tropical Plants|website=tropical.theferns.info|access-date=2019-07-25}}</ref> When used as a fence, it can be impervious to animals due to its spiny nature.<ref name=":2" />

==Taxonomy==
First described as ''Cereus griseus'' in 1812 by Adrian Hardy Haworth, the species was later placed in the genus ''Stenocereus'' by Franz Buxbaum in 1961.<ref name="Haworth 1812 p. 182">{{cite book | last=Haworth | first=A.H. | title=Synopsis Plantarum Succulentarum: Cum Descriptionibus, Synonymis, Locis, Observationibus Anglicanis, Culturaque | publisher=Typis Richardi Taylor et Socii | year=1812 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Wg8AAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA182 | language=la | access-date=2024-03-31 | page=182}}</ref> The specific epithet "griseus" derives from Latin, meaning 'gray,' in reference to the thorns of the species. The species is found in CITES Appendix II as a species of Least Concern. Its population is considered stable.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://eol.org/pages/5184499|title=Stenocereus griseus (Haw.) Buxb. - Encyclopedia of Life|website=eol.org|access-date=2019-07-25}}</ref>
